intro.title: Care and a boundary
paragraphs: Mum is asking about your move again. Her care is real, but the pressure feels heavy. You want to keep the closeness and your right to decide.
Choose what to say. If an answer doesn’t work, you stay where you are, see the reaction and understand why.
intro.note: The other person’s styles are patterns of behaviour, not types of people: the same person acts differently on different days. Real people react differently, so this is practice with wording, not a prediction.
intro.disclaimer: A learning simulation. The material draws on well-known communication methods (sources are given at each step), but it has not yet been reviewed by a psychologist.

variants.name: Critical and touchy
variants.desc: Compares, reproaches and is easily offended.

nodes.narr: Sunday, your parents’ kitchen. Tea, pie — and Mum’s question about your plans. Conversations like this used to end in hurt feelings.

options.text: Mum, I understand you’re worried. I’ll tell you what I’m deciding, but the decision stays mine.
options.why: You acknowledge Mum’s feelings and at the same time clearly name the boundary: “the decision is mine”. It’s not a refusal of closeness but a clarification of roles.

direct.say: Oh… well, all right. Tell me.

evasive.say: Well… suppose so. Go on.

options.text: Stay out of my life!
options.why: A harsh phrase turns care, however clumsy, into an attack. Mum will feel hurt, not a boundary.

direct.say: What a tone! I’m your mother, I’m allowed to worry.

evasive.say: So that’s how you talk to your mother…

options.text: I’m not thinking anything, everything’s fine.
options.why: Hiding the topic leaves the tension. Mum will sense something unsaid and keep asking.

direct.say: You’re not telling me something…

evasive.say: There you go, closing off again.

options.text: Explain in detail: the salary, the city, the friends, every reason.
options.why: A detailed report gives Mum the right to judge every decision. You don’t have to prove your decision is “good enough”.

direct.say: Those are all weak reasons. Suit yourself.

evasive.say: But it could have been done differently…

options.text: You’re right, maybe it’s better to stay.
options.why: Agreeing just to end the conversation only postpones the conflict. You’ll have to decide again, now with the feeling you weren’t heard.

direct.say: You see, Mum won’t give bad advice.

evasive.say: There, that’s right, should have done it long ago.

tech.name: Describe, express, assert
tech.text: Acknowledge the other person’s feelings and clearly state your position in a calm tone, without excuses.

nodes.hint: How to acknowledge Mum’s feelings and still keep the right to decide for yourself?

direct.say: So, are you still thinking about this move? I didn’t sleep all night.

evasive.say: These plans of yours again. Others your age have already settled down.

nodes.narr: Mum goes on. Now about what might go wrong.

options.text: When we discuss the move and I hear predictions of failure, I get more anxious. I need your support. For now, could you just ask how I’m preparing?
options.why: The structure of nonviolent communication: observation, feeling, need, request. You name what’s happening to you and ask for something specific, without blame.

direct.say: All right… tell me how you’re preparing.

evasive.say: Go on then… tell me.

options.text: You always doubt me.
options.why: The generalisation “always” sounds like an accusation and triggers defensiveness. The conversation drifts into an argument about who feels what.

direct.say: I don’t doubt you! I worry, that’s different.

evasive.say: No, not at all, I just want the best.

options.text: If it doesn’t work out, it doesn’t. I’ll survive.
options.why: Sarcasm and bravado shut the conversation down: Mum hears coldness, not a request for support.

direct.say: How hard you’ve become.

evasive.say: Oh, what a tone.

options.text: Let’s talk about something else: how’s your blood pressure?
options.why: An abrupt change of subject leaves the conflict unresolved: Mum will come back to it later, and you’ll feel unheard again.

direct.say: Don’t dodge the conversation.

evasive.say: There you go, wriggling out again.

tech.name: Observation, feeling, need, request
tech.text: Talk about what you see and feel and ask for a specific action, without blaming.

nodes.hint: How to say what you need without blaming?

direct.say: And what if it doesn’t work out there? Who will help you?

evasive.say: You always give up on what you start.

nodes.narr: Mum moves to the hardest part: feelings.

options.text: Thank you for caring. I know you mean well, but the decision will still be mine.
options.why: You acknowledge the care without giving up your decision. Gratitude and a boundary can sound in one sentence.

direct.say: Well… all right. I’m trying to understand.

evasive.say: OK. But this is hard for me.

options.text: You’re manipulating me!
options.why: The label “manipulation” causes hurt and defensiveness. Even if you’re right, an argument about intentions takes you off topic.

direct.say: How can you say that to your mother!

evasive.say: Well, thank you, now I’m a manipulator.

options.text: Sorry, I don’t want to hurt you. Let’s forget it all.
options.why: Asking to “forget it” devalues your boundary. Mum will decide she can carry on, and you’ll be left with the same question.

direct.say: Good, so you’re not going.

evasive.say: Good, that’s better.

options.text: I need a pause. Let’s continue tomorrow.
options.why: A time-out is appropriate if emotions are too strong: you’re not running away, you’re setting a time to come back. Stronger: first say that you heard her.

direct.say: All right. Tomorrow it is.

evasive.say: Well… let’s do tomorrow.

tech.name: Acknowledge and hold
tech.text: Acknowledge a loved one’s feelings and repeat your decision without arguing about intentions.

nodes.hint: How to respond to being called ungrateful?

direct.say: I only want the best for you. I’m your mum, it hurts me.

evasive.say: Ingratitude — that’s what I get for everything.

nodes.narr: The tension has eased. What remains is what Mum really wants to keep: the connection.
nodes.ask: How do you reach an agreement?

options.text: Let’s agree: I’ll call on Sunday evenings and text when I arrive. Does that work?
options.why: A realistic agreement is better than promises that are hard to keep: it eases Mum’s anxiety and keeps your independence.

direct.say: Sunday evenings… all right, I’ll be waiting.

evasive.say: At least that. OK.

options.text: Of course, I’ll call every day!
options.why: A promise you can’t keep will create new hurt. Better to name what’s realistic.

direct.say: Every day? That’s good. Don’t forget.

evasive.say: Really? Well, mind you, every day.

options.text: Don’t demand anything from me.
options.why: Refusing any agreement reads as coldness. The closeness is left without a form.

direct.say: There you go. I can’t even ask.

evasive.say: Of course, who am I, I’m nobody.

options.text: We’ll see.
options.why: A vague answer leaves the anxiety open: Mum is left imagining the worst.

direct.say: What does “we’ll see” mean?

evasive.say: “We’ll see” again… I knew it.

tech.name: A realistic agreement
tech.text: Agree on a specific rhythm of contact you can keep.

nodes.hint: How to suggest a way of staying in touch you can actually manage?

direct.say: All right… but you’ll call? At least once a day?

evasive.say: Well, fine. But don’t expect me to be happy about it.

nodes.narr: The main thing has been said. Now choose how to finish.
nodes.ask: What do you say as you leave?

options.text: Thanks for listening. It matters to me that you know: I love you, and that doesn’t change.
options.why: A warm phrase after a hard conversation brings back closeness. A boundary doesn’t cancel love — it helps it last.

direct.say: I love you too. Take care.

evasive.say: Well… I love you too. Call me.

options.text: You see, everything’s fine.
options.why: This sounds like a victory and may sting. It’s better to end with warmth than with the outcome of an argument.

direct.say: Well, fine… If that’s how it seems to you.

evasive.say: What’s fine? Nothing is fine.

options.text: The main thing is that you’re not upset.
options.why: Asking someone “not to be upset” shifts responsibility for their feelings. Mum has the right to be sad, and you can bear that.

direct.say: Not be upset… I’ll try.

evasive.say: I’m not upset. I’m just sad.

options.text: OK, I’ll go.
options.why: Leaving without a warm phrase leaves an aftertaste of coldness, even though the talk went well.

direct.say: Go. See you.

evasive.say: Well, go.

tech.name: Strengthen the connection
tech.text: End a difficult conversation with words of closeness: a boundary and love don’t contradict each other.

nodes.hint: How to finish so the closeness remains?

direct.say: All right… you’re so independent.

evasive.say: Do as you see fit.

direct.say: Off you go, the pie is getting cold.

evasive.say: OK. Call on Sunday.

finale.title: Care and a boundary
finale.lead: Mum was heard, the boundary was named, there’s an agreement. Here’s what it relied on:
carry: Acknowledging a loved one’s feelings and still keeping the decision your own.
Speaking in “I” statements and asking for something specific instead of blaming.
Agreeing on a rhythm of contact you can really keep.
finale.prompt: How would this sound in your conversation with someone close? Write down your version to come back to before you meet.
